S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any fire, thermal runaway, or other overheating event involving a battery, whether or not it caused injury or property damage, within 24 hours of becoming aware of it. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 5 business days when an incident indicates a material risk requiring action, and immediately where an imminent hazard requires urgent action.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each battery model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and a statistically adequate, representative sample. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notification to the regulator, a corrective-action plan, and retesting after changes. ... exceeding 5% does not by itself prohibit sale or require a market ban. ... Before purchase, customers must be given the model’s 55 °C test failure rate and relevant context ... Individual per-model test failure rates need not be published to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units must support secure remote emergency shut-off by the effective date set by the regulator. For units already installed, manufacturers must provide remote shut-off capability through retrofit or replacement within 6 years of the standard taking effect, where technically feasible. Manufacturers must submit a deployment plan and provide customers with clear instructions for any interim safety measures.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery units must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard is adopted. Manufacturers must provide the regulator with an implementation plan and evidence that the suppression system is effective, reliable, and does not introduce other safety hazards.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan. The regulator shall promptly assess the risk and corrective progress and may require a recall ... Exceeding the threshold alone does not automatically require a recall or sales ban; regulators may order either where warranted.

document.section_notes: S1 is strict: all incidents reported within 24h, customer notice within 5 business days. S2 sets 55°C/5% but does not stop sales above the limit and keeps public per-model rates confidential. S3 requires new-unit shut-off by the effective date and a 6-year retrofit with a feasibility escape. S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months. S5 has an 8/100k notification/corrective-action trigger but recall is discretionary, with an open-ended corrective alternative.
